reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant disorder classically caused by variants in the PNKD gene (MR1) on chromosome 2, encoding a protein related to stress-response and detoxification pathways
Attacks are not triggered by sudden movement but are provoked by alcohol, caffeine, stress, fatigue or excitement
Episodes are longer than in kinesigenic dyskinesia, typically lasting minutes to hours, and occur less frequently, often only a few times per week or month
The movement disorder is a mixed dystonia and chorea that can involve the limbs, trunk and face, with preserved consciousness
Onset is usually in infancy or childhood and a strong autosomal dominant family history is common
Response to sodium-channel-blocking anticonvulsants is generally poor, in contrast to kinesigenic dyskinesia, and trigger avoidance is a mainstay
Benzodiazepines such as clonazepam may help abort or reduce attacks in some patients
reference.pathophysiology: Paroxysmal non-kinesigenic dyskinesia is classically caused by heterozygous variants in the PNKD gene (also called MR1) on chromosome 2, which encodes a protein homologous to hydroxyacylglutathione hydrolase involved in cellular defence against oxidative and metabolic stress, including by-products of alcohol and caffeine metabolism. Impaired handling of these stressors is thought to transiently destabilise striatal neuronal function, producing prolonged episodes of dystonia and chorea after exposure to recognised triggers. The distinct molecular mechanism explains why attacks are provoked by ingested triggers rather than movement and why they respond poorly to sodium-channel blockade.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary paroxysmal dyskinesia (multiple sclerosis, structural lesion)
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI to exclude a secondary structural cause
Electroencephalography to distinguish from epileptic events
SLC2A1 testing and cerebrospinal fluid glucose analysis where exercise-induced attacks suggest GLUT1 deficiency
Metabolic and autoimmune screen when a secondary cause is suspected
Attack diary correlating episodes with dietary and lifestyle triggers
redFlags: New onset in adulthood or progressive course suggesting a secondary or structural cause
Loss of awareness during attacks pointing to seizures
Abnormal brain imaging requiring further evaluation
reference.prognosis: PNKD is a benign, non-degenerative disorder; while attacks are longer and less responsive to medication than in the kinesigenic form, avoidance of triggers substantially reduces frequency and many patients see attacks lessen over time.
pitfalls: Expecting a good response to sodium-channel blockers as seen in kinesigenic dyskinesia and escalating therapy inappropriately
Failing to identify and counsel on alcohol and caffeine as key triggers
Confusing prolonged attacks with focal seizures or functional episodes
Overlooking GLUT1 deficiency when exercise rather than ingestion is the main precipitant
